title: Cast thy bread (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
hookLine: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days"
carry: thou knowest not which shall prosper

cards: Bread, tossed from a riverbank onto moving water. It floats a second, turns, and the current takes it. By any normal reckoning, that bread is gone.

Nobody gets a receipt from a river. Yet near the end of Ecclesiastes, the book that kept saying all is breath, comes this odd instruction: "Cast thy bread upon the waters, For thou shalt find it after many days."
Let it go, says the teacher, and it will come back to you.

teach.h: HOW IT COMES BACK IS NEVER SAID.
teach.b: The verse never says how the bread comes back, or when, beyond after many days. So readers fill the gap in different ways. Some hear a merchant's advice: send your goods across the sea, and the profit returns in time.
Some hear charity: give to people who can never repay you, and the good finds its way home. The commentator Rashi reads it as kindness done for someone you expect never to see again.

The next verse keeps the hand open: "Divide a portion into seven, yea, even into eight; For thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth." Not one gift, carefully placed. Seven shares, and then one more.

teach.h: WHO WATCHES THE WIND WON'T SOW.
teach.b: Then Kohelet turns to the person who waits for perfect conditions: "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; And he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap."
Stand in the field checking the sky, and the seed stays in the bag.

Then the line that ties it together: "In the morning sow thy seed, And in the evening withhold not thy hand; For thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that." Notice what the teacher doesn't promise.
He doesn't say every gift returns.

teach.h: YOU DON'T KNOW, SO KEEP GIVING.
teach.b: He says you don't know. That not-knowing, which earlier in the book made everything feel like breath, becomes here the reason to keep giving. The bread on the water isn't an investment with a guaranteed return.

how: Some Jewish commentators read Ecclesiastes 11:1 as a teaching about kindness and tzedakah given with no promise of return; in some communities the book of Ecclesiastes is read aloud in synagogue on Sukkot.

o: to give and let go, not knowing what will grow
to plant only when the weather looks right
to save up carefully until the harvest is sure

games.q: cast thy bread — tap the pairs.
p: kindness to someone you won't see again

s: Ecclesiastes promises that every gift will come back
the teacher says you don't know which will prosper. the not-knowing is the point.
the verse never says how the bread returns
only 'after many days.' readers have filled in the how.
Kohelet says to wait for good weather before sowing
he says the one who observes the wind shall not sow.

games.q: you've got bread in your hand and a river in front of you. Kohelet is watching. what does he tell you?
o: keep it. bread in the hand is safer.
wait until the current looks right.
games.why: 'cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days.' and he warns that whoever watches the wind never sows.

practice: Let one small gift come to mind that you could give with no way to know where it lands: a kind word to a stranger, a donation no one will thank you for, an honest compliment to someone you may never see again.
Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold bread before you toss it, and decide not to stand on the bank watching the water afterward. If you pray, you can send the gift off with a word of prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sow. Ecclesiastes' advice to give and let go, casting your bread and sowing your seed before you know what will grow. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew of Ecclesiastes 11:1: send your bread out upon the face of the waters.

carryVoice: Your line: thou knowest not which shall prosper. Bread on the water is a gift, not a loan. See you tomorrow.
